subject: Business Models
title: Longevity as a Business
description: One-minute skill: Longevity as a Business.

hook.text: The global longevity market is projected to reach $600 billion by 2025. Living longer is now an industry.

buildup.text: Companies sell anti-aging supplements, genetic testing, personalized medicine, and biohacking devices.

discovery.text: Bryan Johnson spends $2 million/year on his 'Don't Die' longevity protocol. He's become an industry figurehead.

twist.text: Most longevity products lack rigorous clinical evidence. The market runs on hope and early science, not proven results.

climax.text: If longevity science delivers, every industry—from insurance to retirement—must restructure for 120-year lifespans.

punchline.text: $600B market, mostly unproven science. Longevity sells hope cheaper than proof.

quiz.question: What is the biggest challenge in the longevity industry?
options: Most products lack rigorous clinical evidence

details.summary: Longevity businesses develop products and services aimed at extending healthy human lifespan through anti-aging therapies, supplements, diagnostic testing, and lifestyle optimization..
details.whyItMatters: The longevity market is projected to reach 600 billion dollars as aging populations and billionaire investors pour resources into life extension..
takeaways: Products and services targeting healthy lifespan extension form a growing market
The sector spans from consumer supplements to clinical anti-aging therapies
Billionaire investment and aging demographics are accelerating market growth

faq.question: What business categories exist in the longevity market?
faq.answer: Consumer supplements like NMN and resveratrol. Biological age testing from companies like TruDiagnostic. Clinical therapies targeting cellular aging mechanisms. Longevity-focused health clinics offering comprehensive optimization programs. Data platforms tracking aging biomarkers over time.

faq.question: How much scientific evidence supports longevity business products?
faq.answer: Clinical anti-aging therapies have promising animal data but limited human trial results. Caloric restriction and exercise have the strongest evidence. Many consumer supplements lack rigorous proof of efficacy in humans..
